source.title: Relating Regularization and Generalization through the Intrinsic Dimension of Activations
source.authors: B. Brown; Jordan Juravsky; Anthony L. Caterini; G. Loaiza-Ganem

page_placements.theme: Memorization changes representation, activation and spectral diagnostics

record.tranche_reason: The study measures activation intrinsic dimension and generalization under regularization and during grokking. Those results bear on whether regularization prevents fitting random labels, but it does not run the random-label, unstructured-input, or noisy-label experiments named in the versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports that all image-classification models achieve perfect training accuracy, but does not report training on random labels or test error at chance. It tests regularization effects on activation ID and validation performance, not whether regularizers prevent fitting random labels. Grokking results concern modular division, not random labeling.
record.test_reason: The study cites Zhang et al. for the success of overparameterized networks, but its own experiments concern activation intrinsic dimension on true-label CIFAR tasks and modular-division grokking. It neither tests nor uses random-label fitting. Its regularization sweeps do not test removal of explicit regularization, the other component of V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: regularization decreases LLID; improved generalization correlates with lower LLID and sufficiently high PID; excessive regularization can impair early feature extraction; and grokking co-occurs with a sudden LLID drop. These are correlational findings, not evidence about random-label fitting.
record.recipe_differences: Measures activation intrinsic dimension and generalization under regularization and during modular-division grokking; does not reproduce the original random-label intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Regularization strength, dataset, and training-set size affect the reported outcomes; the paper notes excessive regularization reduces PID and validation accuracy, and grokking timing depends on weight decay and training-set size.

fits_no_version.finding: On true-label CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, stronger weight decay or dropout decreases LLID. Validation accuracy correlates with higher PID/LLID, while excessive regularization reduces PID and validation accuracy despite perfect training accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation intrinsic dimension correlates with generalization across regularization settings in ResNet-18 image classifiers.

fits_no_version.finding: Modular-division transformers exhibit LLID drops alongside grokking; average minimum LLID is 8.53 for grokking models versus 16.16 for models remaining at low validation accuracy within 40,000 steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking in small modular-division transformers co-occurs with reduced activation LLID.

record.code_released: The authors state that code will be released publicly upon acceptance; no URL stated.
record.peer_reviewed: OPT2022: 14th Annual Workshop on Optimization for Machine Learning
record.problems: The paper uses estimated intrinsic dimension and acknowledges that the estimator can produce apparent increases across layers despite true ID not increasing. Several image-classification trends are presented in figures without exact values in the text. The study does not test the random-label claim directly.
record.rows_left_out: No results relevant to the six versions were omitted. Figure-only numerical values were not reconstructed.

untested.parts: All parts: no completely random labels, chance test error, or matched training recipe comparison.
All parts: no true-versus-random-label fitting times or corruption-dependent convergence measurements.
All parts: no shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.
All parts: no label-corruption sweep or associated training and test error curves.
Neither random-label fitting under explicit regularization nor true-label generalization after removing explicit regularization is tested. CIFAR data augmentation remains in use.
All parts: no comparison of shared real-data pattern learning with noisy or random-label memorization.

record.verdict_notes: The record's tests/T2 classification conflicts with its correctly unlinked rows and should be replaced by cites_only/T6. No verdict on V1–V6 is warranted.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling, chance test error, or unchanged-architecture/hyperparameter random-label test.
No comparison of training time or convergence speed for true versus random labels, or by corruption fraction.
No shuffled-pixel, independently permuted-pixel, or Gaussian-noise input experiments.
No sweep over fractions of corrupted labels or measurement of training and test error across that sweep.

The study varies weight decay and dropout and reports true-label training and validation performance, but does not test random-label fitting or whether removing regularization alone makes true-label generalization poor.
No comparison of learning dynamics for real versus noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Swept weight decay and dropout independently during CIFAR training; measured final LLID.

conditions.value: varying weight decay or dropout strength
200 epochs; SGD, momentum 0.9; learning rate 0.1 decayed at epochs 60, 120, 160

rows.measure: Last-layer intrinsic dimension of validation activations; LLID decreases as regularization strength increases.
rows.uncertainty: Pearson correlation coefficients and t-test p-values are shown in Figure 1; exact values not stated in supplied text.
rows.note: Figure caption and Results text describe the trend, but no numeric LLID values or exact correlation statistics are given in text.
rows.check: The decreasing LLID trend is explicitly reported, but measures representational complexity on true-label data rather than any claim version. Missing numerical figure values do not make the trend itself indeterminate.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared PID and LLID with validation accuracy across regularization settings.
rows.measure: Association between PID/LLID ratio and validation accuracy; higher ratio is described as indicating better validation performance.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes a clear trend, but does not provide exact values.
rows.check: The reported PID/LLID association with validation accuracy measures a different construct and cannot establish any version's effect.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Compared PID and validation accuracy under excessive regularization.

conditions.value: beyond the value giving optimal validation accuracy

rows.measure: PID and validation accuracy decrease as regularization is increased beyond the optimum; training accuracy remains near-perfect according to the abstract.
rows.note: The results describe rapid declines in PID and validation accuracy under excessive regularization. All image-classification models are stated to achieve perfect training accuracy.
rows.check: Excessive regularization reduces PID and true-label validation accuracy; this does not test random-label fitting or removing regularization. Section 3.1 states perfect training accuracy for all image models, stronger than the abstract's near-perfect wording.

rows.subject: two-layer transformer models
rows.operation_detail: Tracked LLID and validation accuracy during modular-division training across weight decay and training-set-size settings.
rows.measure: LLID drop co-occurring with sudden validation-accuracy rise in models that grok; models that grok have average minimum LLID 8.53 versus 16.16 for models that remain at low validation accuracy within the compute budget.
rows.baseline: Models remaining at low validation accuracy: average minimum LLID 16.16
rows.value: Models that grok: average minimum LLID 8.53
rows.note: This is a modular-division grokking result, not a random-label experiment. The paper also describes an initial LLID spike in some lower-training-data settings before descent.
rows.check: The LLID averages 8.53 and 16.16 are correctly reported, but modular-division grokking does not compare learning real labels with learning noisy or random labels. Memorization preceding generalization here does not challenge V6.
